title: A Map Is Not a Verdict

scenes.tts: Where in the brain does a function live? Start with the map. From the side, the cerebral cortex divides into four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital. The brainstem and the cerebellum sit beside them. A map names places. It does not tell you what lives in each one.
scenes.visual: Lateral view of the left side of the brain: the four lobes, brainstem and cerebellum appear as they are named; a question mark ends the scene.
scenes.narration: Where in the brain does a function live? Start with the map. From the side, the cerebral cortex divides into four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital. The brainstem and the cerebellum sit beside them. A map names places. It does not tell you what lives in each one.

scenes.tts: Read the map literally. The precentral gyrus contains primary motor cortex. The postcentral gyrus contains primary somatosensory cortex. No region here has a single function, and no function lives in a single region. The cortex is a mosaic. One atlas of healthy young adults divides each hemisphere into one hundred eighty areas, and borders vary between people.
scenes.visual: Same lateral view: two gyri highlighted, then a mosaic overlay with the atlas count; labels never claim one function per region.

scenes.tts: So what kind of experiment can place a function? The first is a lesion. You compare behaviour after damage with a baseline or controls. A deficit shows the damaged tissue contributes to the task. But damage spreads. In a 1957 report on human patients, several medial temporal structures were removed at once. The memory loss could not be pinned to one.
scenes.visual: Several unnamed structure boxes; a damage cloud covers all of them; a deficit box follows; the question of which structure stays open.
scenes.narration: So what kind of experiment can place a function? The first is a lesion. You compare behaviour after damage with a baseline or controls. scenes.tts: The second kind is a recording. Firing goes with a stimulus or a choice. That does not show the brain uses it. The third kind is imaging. A BOLD f M R I signal measures blood oxygenation. In anaesthetized macaque visual cortex, it followed local field potentials better than spiking. An activation does not mark a region as the seat of anything.
scenes.visual: Left: a firing sketch rises with a stimulus bar, then a question about use. Right: three boxes, BOLD followed local field potentials more closely than spiking.

scenes.tts: The fourth kind adds activity. Rhesus monkeys judged the direction of noisy moving dots. Salzman, Newsome and their colleagues applied current in area M T where neurons shared a preferred direction. In one hundred thirty nine experiments, stimulation had a significant effect in eighty nine. In eighty six of those, choices moved toward the preferred direction. That shows a contribution, in that task, from the stimulated neurons, not from one cell type.
scenes.visual: MT neurons with one shared preferred direction receive current pulses; the choice shifts; nested bars 139, 89, 86 build.

scenes.tts: Here is the rule. A lesion shows contribution, not which part of the damage mattered. A recording shows covariation, not use. Imaging shows where a blood signal goes, not which neural signal. Stimulation shows contribution, not that the region is required. Claim only what the evidence licenses.
scenes.visual: Four rows build: kind of evidence, what it can show, what it cannot show alone; the rule line ends the scene.
